content: The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management, specifically the guidelines on Highly Hazardous Pesticides (HHPs), was published by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations and the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2016. The Inter-Organization Programme for the Sound Management of Chemicals (IOMC) was established in 1995 following recommendations from the 1992 UN Conference on Environment and Development. Its purpose is to strengthen international coordination in chemical safety. Participating organizations include FAO, the International Labour Organization (ILO), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR), and WHO. The World Bank and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) are observers. The IOMC promotes coordination of policies and activities pursued by participating organizations to achieve sound chemical management in relation to human health and the environment. This publication was developed within the IOMC context and does not necessarily reflect the views or policies of individual IOMC participating organizations. The guidelines expand upon articles addressing HHPs in the Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management, aiming to help countries interpret and apply these articles effectively to reduce risks posed by HHPs. Countries are encouraged to identify HHPs in use, assess associated risks, and implement appropriate measures to mitigate these risks. Pesticides requiring personal protective equipment (PPE) that is uncomfortable, expensive, or not readily available should be avoided, particularly for small-scale users and farmworkers in hot climates. Governments should collect reliable data and maintain statistics on the health effects of pesticides and pesticide poisoning incidents, using harmonized tools where available. They should submit relevant data, such as the Rotterdam Convention Human Health Incident Report Forms on Severely Hazardous Pesticide Formulations (SHPF), to the designated national authority. Trained personnel and adequate resources should be made available to ensure the accuracy of collected information. Governments should introduce necessary policies and legislation for the regulation of pesticides throughout their life cycle, including production, authorization, import, distribution, sale, supply, transport, storage, handling, application, and disposal. These measures should ensure safety and efficacy while minimizing adverse health and environmental effects. Governments should also establish appropriate educational, advisory, extension, and healthcare services, using FAO and WHO guidelines and relevant legally binding instruments as a basis. Local needs, social and economic conditions, literacy levels, and climate should be considered in these efforts.
